clinicalPearls: FHH type 2 is a rare autosomal dominant cause of lifelong, generally asymptomatic hypercalcaemia caused by loss-of-function variants in GNA11, which encodes the Gα11 subunit downstream of the calcium-sensing receptor.

It is one of three FHH subtypes: type 1 (CASR mutations, the commonest), type 2 (GNA11), and type 3 (AP2S1), all sharing the biochemical signature of hypercalcaemia with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion.

The defect impairs signal transduction from the calcium-sensing receptor in parathyroid and renal tubular cells, so the calcium set-point is reset upward and the gland behaves as if calcium levels are normal.
The hallmark is a low calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio, which helps distinguish FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism where renal calcium handling is not avidly conservative.
Parathyroid hormone is characteristically normal or only mildly elevated despite hypercalcaemia, and magnesium may be normal or slightly high.
The condition is typically benign and does not cause the nephrolithiasis or bone disease seen in primary hyperparathyroidism, so recognition prevents unnecessary parathyroidectomy.
Genetic testing for a GNA11 variant confirms the diagnosis when CASR sequencing is negative and family biochemistry is consistent with FHH.
FHH2 tends to show milder biochemical derangement than FHH1, and activating GNA11 variants conversely cause the mirror-image disorder of autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 2.
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia type 2 arises from heterozygous inactivating (loss-of-function) variants in GNA11, the gene encoding the alpha subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein Gα11. Gα11 lies immediately downstream of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a G-protein-coupled receptor expressed on the surface of parathyroid chief cells and the renal tubule that continuously monitors extracellular ionised calcium. When calcium binds the CaSR, the receptor normally couples through Gα11 (and Gαq) to activate phospholipase C, generating inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, mobilising intracellular calcium and thereby suppressing parathyroid hormone secretion while promoting urinary calcium excretion. A defective Gα11 subunit blunts this transduction, so the parathyroid gland and kidney sense a falsely low calcium concentration and the homeostatic set-point is shifted upward. The parathyroid gland therefore continues to secrete parathyroid hormone at inappropriately normal or mildly elevated levels for the prevailing hypercalcaemia, and the renal tubule avidly reabsorbs calcium, producing the paradoxical combination of hypercalcaemia with hypocalciuria. Because the underlying receptor pathway remains structurally intact and the disturbance is one of set-point rather than of autonomous glandular overactivity, the disorder is lifelong, familial and generally free of end-organ calcium-related damage.
additionalDifferentials: FHH type 1 due to CASR loss-of-function variants
FHH type 3 due to AP2S1 variants
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease
Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia including PTH-related peptide secretion
Vitamin D excess or granulomatous hypercalcaemia
additionalInvestigations: Simultaneous serum calcium, ionised calcium and parathyroid hormone measurement
Calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio from paired serum and 24-hour urine samples
GNA11 gene sequencing, with CASR and AP2S1 analysis to exclude other FHH subtypes
Family biochemical screening across first-degree relatives to establish an inheritance pattern
Vitamin D metabolites and PTH-related peptide where malignancy or vitamin D excess is considered
Medication review to exclude lithium and thiazide effects on calcium handling
redFlags: Escalating hypercalcaemia with symptoms suggesting an alternative or coexisting cause such as malignancy
Development of nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis or overt bone disease, which is atypical and points away from simple FHH
Severe neonatal hypercalcaemia in the offspring of two affected parents indicating a homozygous or biallelic state
Biochemistry evolving in a way that mimics primary hyperparathyroidism and risks inappropriate surgery
Symptomatic hypercalcaemic crisis requiring urgent evaluation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, as the hypercalcaemia is mild, stable and typically asymptomatic throughout life, without the renal or skeletal complications of primary hyperparathyroidism. The chief risk is iatrogenic harm from misdiagnosis leading to unnecessary parathyroid surgery.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing FHH2 as primary hyperparathyroidism and proceeding to a futile parathyroidectomy
Relying on the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio alone, since values can overlap with primary hyperparathyroidism and be confounded by vitamin D deficiency
Overlooking lithium or thiazide therapy that can reproduce the hypocalciuric hypercalcaemic pattern
Assuming a negative CASR test excludes FHH and failing to test GNA11 and AP2S1
Failing to counsel relatives about the autosomal dominant inheritance and the benign natural history
